title: Cloud-native event-driven microservices platform
description: A conceptual order platform with five views covering system context, service boundaries, event delivery, Kubernetes operations, and infrastructure provisioning.

views.title: System context
views.summary: A shopper places an order from a web or mobile client. The order platform authenticates the request, coordinates payment through an external provider, and sends updates through a notification provider.
notes: Entry point
A cloud load balancer or API gateway accepts HTTPS traffic. An ingress controller routes requests to Kubernetes Services inside the platform boundary.
Availability
Distribute replicas across failure domains and choose managed data services with recovery objectives that fit the system. A redundant API tier still depends on the datastore and external providers.
Network boundaries

Keep workloads and managed data endpoints on private network paths where possible. Restrict provider egress and rehearse failover and restore procedures against the required recovery time and data loss limits.

views.title: Microservices and data ownership
views.summary: Java and Spring Boot services own distinct business capabilities. Each service can deploy independently and owns its writes. Shared hosting can still use separate credentials and logical databases.
notes: Domain ownership

Order owns order state, Payment owns payment attempts, Notification owns delivery records, and Identity owns identity concerns. A bounded context defines its terms and invariants before it becomes a deployment boundary.
REST or messaging

Use synchronous calls when the caller needs an immediate answer. Use events for background work when consumers can tolerate delayed updates. HTTP contracts need versioning as callers evolve, and timeouts bound the effect of downstream delays.
Data and failure isolation

Use local transactions and design cross-service changes for eventual consistency. For example, a failed payment can trigger an order cancellation through a saga. Redis can cache read models with explicit expiry and invalidation while PostgreSQL remains the source of truth.

views.title: Publishing and consuming an order event
views.summary: The order write and its outbox record commit in one database transaction. A relay publishes the outbox record to Kafka. A Payment consumer processes the order event, then emits a payment outcome that a Notification consumer handles independently.
notes: Ordering and parallelism

Key order events by order ID to preserve their order within a topic partition. Consumer groups share partitions, while separate groups advance independently. Ordering across partitions or topics requires explicit business handling.
Duplicate delivery

At-least-once processing can redeliver an event after a crash, and the outbox relay can publish twice. Persist processed IDs with local side effects where possible, and commit offsets after durable processing. An external payment still needs a provider idempotency key or reconciliation when the result is uncertain.
Retry and replay

Bound retry attempts with backoff and route exhausted or invalid events to a dead-letter topic for investigation. Moving a failed event to a retry topic can let later events overtake it. Plan schema compatibility and deduplication retention before replay.

views.title: Kubernetes deployment and runtime
views.summary: An ingress controller and Services route traffic to healthy Pods. Deployments manage replica sets and rolling changes. A registry supplies versioned Docker images for the workloads.
notes: Configuration and identity

Use ConfigMaps for non-sensitive configuration. Scope Secrets and service-account access with RBAC and limit traffic with network policies. Decide whether state belongs in managed services or persistent volumes when setting recovery and portability requirements.
Health and scale

Use readiness probes to remove unready endpoints and liveness probes for stuck processes. Resource requests guide scheduling and CPU-based scaling. Limits constrain usage, and an HPA can scale from resource or workload metrics such as consumer lag.
Rolling deployment

Set rollout capacity and disruption budgets with replica count and availability goals in mind. Observe readiness and errors during promotion. Revert a failed release to a known version, with an explicit plan for migration compatibility.

views.title: Application delivery and infrastructure provisioning
views.summary: Application and infrastructure pipelines have different lifecycles. Docker packages the application, a registry stores the image, Helm manages its Kubernetes release, and Terraform manages cloud resources.

flows.name: Infrastructure pipeline
nodes: Cloud network, cluster and managed services

notes: Docker and the registry
Build in stages and copy only runtime artifacts into the final image. Scan and promote the same immutable digest between environments. Runtime configuration and credentials arrive at deployment time.
Helm and Kubernetes

Keep workload templates and defaults in a versioned chart with environment-specific values supplied during release. Helm tracks the release revision. Kubernetes reconciles the workload, and deployment automation watches health and decides whether to roll back.
Terraform

Providers manage APIs for cloud resources. Modules, environment-specific variables, and outputs describe reusable infrastructure and dependencies. Use isolated remote state, locking where supported, and a reviewed plan before applying. Application release automation can evolve independently of cluster provisioning.
